rv.q: I defy anyone not to fall in love with it.
Complex ideas about love, literature, body image and truth are expressed in its dizzyingly clever rhymes, but essentially it remains a captivating, tragicomic romance.
There is nothing fey or decorative.
And yet, this noseless revival, adapted by Martin Crimp into modern, rap-inspired English verse, is the best play I’ve seen all year.

Anyone who knows Cyrano de Bergerac knows it’s about the nose. It’s one of the most famous hooters in history: curse of its hero and of theatre designers alike. Not in Jamie Lloyd’s dazzling reboot of Edmond Rostand’s poignant verse romance, however.

I feel more sure of myself in declaring the show – which kicks off a season of Jamie Lloyd productions at the Playhouse that includes Jessica Chastain’s West End debut in Ibsen’s A Doll’s House – inspired in its minimalist eloquence.
McAvoy’s performance is intense and emotive, even if he doesn’t totally convince as someone no woman would want to touch.

Lloyd’s production makes you see an old play with fresh eyes and the opening image, in Soutra Gilmour’s stark design, of Cyrano staring fixedly at himself in a mirror, turns Rostand’s comedy into a study in physical and linguistic self-regard.
This is a great production of something – but it’s not Cyrano De Bergerac.

Ugly but clever Cyrano, a soldier with a huge nose, sees he has no chance of winning the heart of Roxane because she prefers dim, handsome Christian. Cyrano helps Christian to court Roxane, wooing her by proxy. Much of Martin Crimp’s new text is in rap, and there is a striking title performance by James McAvoy.
This time, McAvoy comes up with a breathtaking career-best performance, and the entire evening is a dazzling triumph.
It is a triumph, a breathtakingly bold rethinking of a classic in resonant contemporary ways.
I wouldn't necessarily want all my classics to be delivered in this way, but Lloyd's company is committed to attracting a youthful audience...
It’s late in the day, but this is a last-minute contender for production of the year.

cn.t: Critics hail Jamie Lloyd's radical, stripped-back Cyrano as electrifying theatre, with McAvoy's powerhouse performance and Crimp's rap-inspired verse earning widespread praise, though some purists dismiss the no-nose approach as gimmicky.
